assessment.nobel_worthiness: GLP-1 physiology, from the incretin effect and proglucagon processing to receptor biology, led to incretin-based drugs that transformed treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity. The discovery chain is clear, original and has very large, still-growing clinical and physiological impact, including central appetite pathways relevant to neuroscience.
assessment.attribution: Holst (physiology of native GLP-1 and its insulinotropic action) and Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology, therapeutic translation) are core. Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is a decisive early contribution but credit is contested; Knudsen led the development of liraglutide/semaglutide, and Habener is not on the supplied list, so a three-person configuration necessarily omits someone important.
assessment.maturity: Mature: decades of replication, multiple approved drugs with outcome trials in cardiovascular, renal and weight endpoints. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Fair split between basic discoverers and drug developers is unresolved.
Mojsov credit dispute and Habener's absence from the credited names complicate the three-person limit.
I rely on my own recollection of the literature and have not verified details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rational design and clinical proof of BCR-ABL kinase inhibition with imatinib turned chronic myeloid leukemia from a fatal disease into a manageable one and established the paradigm of molecularly targeted cancer therapy. Importance, clarity and lasting impact are exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Lydon (compound program and target selection), Druker (clinical translation and proof of concept) and Sawyers (resistance mechanisms and second-generation inhibitors) form a coherent trio. Rowley, Nowell and Hungerford (Philadelphia chromosome) and the Witte/Baltimore/Wang ABL work, and Zimmermann as chemist, are outside the credited names, so the earlier lineage is not recognized.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: long-term survival data over two decades, widespread replication, many successor drugs.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should instead recognize earlier cytogenetic and oncogene work.
Allocation relative to medicinal chemists is partly outside the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Engineered CAR-T cells created a new class of living drugs with durable remissions in refractory B-cell malignancies. This is a clear conceptual and clinical breakthrough with growing extension to autoimmune disease.
assessment.attribution: June (clinical CD19 CAR-T, CD28/4-1BB-based constructs in patients), Sadelain (second-generation CAR design and costimulation) and Rosenberg (adoptive cell therapy, TIL and early gene-modified T cells) are plausible. Eshhar, Gross and others who devised the chimeric receptor concept are not on the supplied list, which weakens the fairness of the configuration.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature with approved products and multi-year follow-up, though solid-tumor success, toxicity and long-term safety are still developing.
uncertainties: Early conceptual credit (chimeric receptor origin) not captured in the supplied names.
Long-term durability and secondary malignancy signals remain under study.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Antisense correction of SMN2 splicing (nusinersen) gave the first effective disease-modifying therapy for spinal muscular atrophy, converting a lethal infantile neurogenetic disease into a treatable one. The mechanistic logic is clean and the clinical effect is dramatic; it validates RNA-targeted therapeutics broadly.
assessment.attribution: Krainer (splicing mechanism and ASO design for SMN2 exon 7 inclusion) and Bennett (ASO chemistry and drug development) are the natural pair. Lamond-type SMN biology and the discovery of the SMN1 gene by Melki and colleagues are outside the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Strong clinical confirmation since 2016 and the field is stable, but the prize may be seen as early relative to the long-term outcomes data.
uncertainties: Whether SMN1 gene discovery deserves co-recognition.
Long-term benefit in treated adults and presymptomatic cohorts is still accumulating.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optogenetics provided a general method for causal control of defined neurons with light and is now foundational across neuroscience. Originality and impact on experimental physiology are very high, though the direct clinical impact is so far limited.
assessment.attribution: Nagel and Hegemann (channelrhodopsin identification and characterization, with Bamberg) and Deisseroth (neuronal implementation, tools, and application) are the central figures. Boyden, Miesenböck and Bamberg have strong claims, and six credited people cannot fit in three, so attribution is the main obstacle.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a technique with thousands of replications. Clinical translation (e.g. retinal optogenetic therapy) is early.
uncertainties: Allocation among at least six credible contributors, including Boyden and Bamberg.
Disputed priority for the first neuronal demonstration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showing that TNF is a therapeutic target in rheumatoid arthritis and that blockade works in patients opened the biologic era for chronic inflammatory disease, with major impact in rheumatology, gastroenterology and dermatology.
assessment.attribution: The Feldmann and Maini partnership is a well-defined two-person credit built on the discovery of TNF's central role in synovial cytokine networks and the first anti-TNF clinical trials. Contributions by Kollias, Cerami and the antibody-engineering teams are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature with decades of clinical use and a strong evidence base; recognition is fitting though biosimilars and newer drug classes have shifted the practice landscape.
uncertainties: Treatment-translation prize may be competing with more basic discoveries.
Role of TNF cloning and antibody development groups in overall credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Identification of tau and alpha-synuclein as the molecular constituents of filamentous pathology in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease (and Lewy bodies) redefined these disorders as proteinopathies and underpins biomarkers, cryo-EM structures and therapeutic trials. As a neurologist I recognize the clinical consequence but weigh it by the same criteria as other candidates.
assessment.attribution: Goedert and Spillantini are a coherent pair, with Spillantini central to alpha-synuclein in Lewy bodies and Goedert to tau and filament characterization. Others (Lee, Trojanowski, Wischik) contributed to adjacent findings and are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Findings are firmly confirmed and have matured into seed-amplification assays and structure-based classification. Disease-modifying therapy based on these targets is still unproven, so recognition may be somewhat premature clinically.
uncertainties: No approved therapy yet that leverages this discovery.
Overlap in priority with other groups that identified amyloid or tau components.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Discovery of TOR as the target of rapamycin and its role as the central regulator of cell growth and nutrient response is a profound conceptual advance with consequences for cancer, metabolism, immunology and ageing.
assessment.attribution: Hall's genetic identification of TOR in yeast is the decisive contribution, and Schreiber's chemical-biology work on rapamycin/FKBP12 supports it. Sabatini, also credited, made later mTORC1 pathway discoveries but I leave him out for a narrower, cleaner configuration. Brown and Sabatini's mammalian mTOR identification and Heitman, Movva and Hall's original findings leave some priority questions.
assessment.maturity: Very well confirmed and conceptually stable; clinical translation through rapalogs is real but moderate.
uncertainties: Whether Sabatini should be included given the broader mTORC1 contributions.
Priority among groups that identified mammalian TOR.
